My goal for the next five years, until I reach 45, is to use AI to help me build a custom trading platform and document my progress as I build my retirement in public.

A post on Saturday, Nov 14 called four websites a must for day and swing trading. Good charts, a stock screener and an economic calendar help a trader read the market.

CloudAi, the automated trading system I built, does a different job: it trades by rules, and its paper results decide how I invest my own money.

1. Built with AI. Claude, Grok, Cursor and Grok Bot run CloudAi, and I use AI to keep building it.
2. Paper first. CloudAi runs on Alpaca in paper mode. On the latest check, its records matched the broker's.
3. Posted in public. I post CloudAi's daily profits and losses on YouTube and other social sites, so the losing days are public too.
4. Profits fund the snowball. The AI system trades every day, moves profits weekly to fund the next snowball rung, and when all 12 rungs are built, I invest my own money exactly according to the results. Dividends from rung 1 flow into rung 2, rung 2 into rung 3, and so on. Snowball #1 filled all 12 rungs, I bought in, and it paid me $2.29 in dividends between Nov 4 and Nov 6. I hold it forever.

TAKEAWAYS: Good tools help a trader. I'm putting my time into building my own with AI. I track the income I actually receive. NFA

What Happens When One Engineer Ships 4,000 Pull Requests a Month: 5 Counter-Intuitive Lessons from Inside the Grok Bot Factory

Most of us still use AI like a secluded intern locked in a basement. We read a bug report in Slack, talk it over with a coworker, copy the context into a coding tool or chat window, babysit the prompt, and paste the result back to our team. We act as the human router between where the conversation happens and where the work gets done.

Lauren Tan and Roman Ugarte got tired of doing that last mile by hand. In just seven weeks, they took Grok Bot from its first line of code to launch, building a platform where AI teammates have their own identities, virtual computers, credentials, and Slack accounts. Along the way, Tan scaled her personal engineering output from 2,000 pull requests a month to over 4,000. 

Looking inside how their team actually builds software and runs their business reveals a set of habits that go against almost every conventional wisdom in tech right now.

1. The Best Place to Write Code Is a Public Slack Thread

When engineers picture a high-velocity coding setup, they usually imagine a developer hunched over an IDE with ten terminal panes open. Tan barely opens her editor for feature work anymore. Recently, she and her colleague Samantha built and shipped an entire feature from start to finish inside a 200-message public Slack thread without Tan ever looking at Cursor or reading the pull request diff.

She simply tagged her personal engineer bot, @poteto , with a link to a video from X. Poteto spun up a cloud agent with its own virtual machine, ran the Grok Bot app empirically like a real user, and posted screenshots and video recordings directly back into the Slack thread for the team to critique. Once the artifact looked right, the agent merged its own code.

Moving agent orchestration out of private, single-player chat windows and into public Slack channels solves an organizational training problem. When someone sees a power user tag a bot in a feedback thread and spin up a working prototype in minutes, they copy that exact workflow the very next day.

   "The more that the stuff is in public, I think the more of the rest of the company that can get lifted up by the top 1% power users who are very tooling minded, very engineering minded, and know exactly how to use these tools."

2. Stop Burning Millions of Tokens on AI Code Reviews

As coding agents write more software, the knee-jerk reaction across the industry has been to throw more AI at the code review step. Host Garry Tan noted that his own software factory burns 30 to 50 million tokens per review trying to catch 30 categories of bugs line by line. Lauren Tan went the opposite direction: she abandoned plan mode entirely and dialed back her multi-model adversarial review skills.

Her reasoning is practical. AI reviewers lack the broader product vision. Left to themselves, reviewing agents overfit on abstract engineering ideals and burn millions of tokens debating edge cases on features that the team plans to deprecate in two months anyway.

Instead of paying agents to argue over every pull request, Tan treats the codebase itself as a form of memory. She invests her time at the top of an inverted pyramid: refactoring architecture, tightening API design, and writing strict static analysis and compiler checks. To keep Grok Bot's Electron desktop app running at a smooth 60 frames per second, tasks on the renderer thread cannot exceed 8 to 16 milliseconds. Rather than relying on human or AI reviewers to spot slow code, the team wrote a dependency graph checker and a custom lint rule that forbids importing between the main and renderer threads.

   "We decided we don't want to think about this problem anymore, we don't want to have to catch it in code review. We'll actually build it as like a lint rule, we built a dependency graph checker, and now it's just enforced by the codebase, enforced by check-in, so it's tokens I don't have to spend anymore."

3. When Code Is Free, Your Real Job Is Refusing to Merge It

For decades, the primary constraint in software was engineering bandwidth. When one person can put up 4,000 pull requests a month, that constraint evaporates. On the Grok Bot team, whenever someone floats a product idea in a meeting, another teammate routinely chimes in to say they already built a pull request for it over the weekend.

That abundance creates a dangerous trap. Merging every working feature simply because the code already exists quickly turns a clean application into a fragmented mess of random side projects. Users hate waking up, refreshing their app, and discovering that core buttons have moved around for the third time that week.

To protect the user experience without slowing down maintenance, the team draws a hard line between bugs and pixels. An automated factory named Sandy ingests thousands of daily complaints from support channels and X, reproduces the bugs, and auto-merges fixes at 3:00 AM with zero human involvement. Core interface changes get the opposite treatment: the team sits with new designs and dogfoods them internally for longer than feels comfortable, killing any update that gets mixed internal feedback.

   "Even though you can go really fast, it doesn't mean that you should just ship every feature you can think of. And this is where human judgment and taste I think comes in."

4. Forget the All-Knowing Super-Bot and Hire an Obsessive Apprentice

Early experiments with autonomous agents often chased the sci-fi dream of a single, omniscient assistant that manages your entire life and business from one prompt. In practice, people and companies find it much easier to organize work around a roster of narrow specialists.

Ugarte models his bots the same way founders hire early employees: you want someone who wakes up thinking about a single problem in the shower rather than one generalist trying to juggle a hundred priorities at once. A domain expert inside the company acts as the manager, training a specialist bot like an apprentice and then sharing that bot with the entire workspace.

This apprentice model explains why small businesses have become some of Grok Bot's most rabid early users. Small business owners struggle acutely with hiring for back-office roles. Out of sheer necessity, they are logging into Grok Bot and configuring dedicated AI employees within a few hours to take over their bookkeeping and accounting.

   "Here's a business problem, I want a bot that cares about that business problem. I want it to be managed by the domain expert at the company who knows the most about that problem so that they can kind of treat it like an apprentice."

5. Non-Technical Teams Are Building Factories, and Goal Specification Is the New Bottleneck

The same loop that powers engineering is now spreading across sales, customer support, data science, and marketing. Grok Bot's performance marketing team gave their bot its own Google Ads and Facebook Ads logins along with a real budget, instructing it to message the design team's bot to generate ad creatives and run A/B tests autonomously. Sales teams share lead-research and deal bots, while support bots parse hundreds of customer messages a minute, resolving routine tickets end-to-end and escalating edge cases to human owners.

Running an automated factory outside of engineering exposes a fascinating structural gap. Software engineers have compilers, test suites, and CPU traces that tell an agent objectively whether its output works, and all the necessary context lives right in the repository. In marketing or operations, there is no compiler, and vital context is usually trapped in people's heads, on paper, or behind a forgotten password.

As organizations flatten toward Jack Dorsey's three-role blueprint of Individual Contributors who ship directly, Directly Responsible Individuals who own outcomes, and Player-Coaches who teach everyone else how to orchestrate bots, middle management disappears. The scarce skill across every department becomes executive function: defining clear KPIs and translating murky human intent into objective functions a bot can measure.

   "In a world where execution is kind of cheap or you could spin up 100 coding agents or 100 Grok Bots to like run at a problem, it really matters that you define the problem well, and the gap is probably not going to be an execution failure, it will probably be an intent specification failure or a goal failure."

Looking Ahead to 2027

By 2027, Tan expects AI teammates to routinely carry their own phone numbers, credit cards, and identities, while brain-computer interfaces like Neuralink's Telepathy could eventually let builders transmit intent to their bot swarms at the literal speed of thought. 

When the friction between having an idea and executing it drops to zero, the advantage will belong entirely to the teams with the discipline to define what is actually worth building.

Key Takeaways

   - Public Multiplayer Loops: Moving agent workflows from single-player editors into shared Slack threads lets agents verify features via visual artifacts while lifting the whole organization's AI skills.   

   - Codebase as Memory: Encoding engineering constraints into compilers, dependency checkers, and lint rules prevents AI slop at zero token cost, outperforming token-heavy AI code reviews.   

   - Intent Over Execution: As specialist bots take over maintenance, bookkeeping, and marketing loops, the human bottleneck shifts to product taste and specifying clear objective functions.

United Airlines just banned AI agents from booking flights.

Not slowed down. Banned.

On November 11, United updated its contract of carriage to block any third-party AI agent from:

→ Booking flights
→ Buying tickets
→ Servicing reservations
→ Even through travel agencies

CEO Scott Kirby's reason: he doesn't want "another middleman."

Meanwhile, Southwest is doing the opposite — letting ChatGPT users browse their flights directly.

This is the first AI agent war.

Companies are splitting into two camps:

Camp 1: Block AI agents (United, Delta)
→ "We control the customer relationship"

Camp 2: Welcome AI agents (Southwest)
→ "Let AI bring us more customers"

This matters because:

→ Grok Bot was just shown rebooking flights by phone
→ OpenAI is building ChatGPT Wallet for purchases
→ AI agents will try to book everything — flights, hotels, food

The companies that block AI agents today will lose customers to the ones that don't.

This is just the beginning.

If I were setting up a Grok Bot team today, I’d give it these 4 instructions on day one.

They cover the things you can spend months correcting one bot at a time. You should be able to open the record behind an answer, see what actually got done and know when a decision needs you.

Copy this into your Chief of Staff:

“Roll out these 4 standing instructions across my bot team. Where a bot already has one, reuse it. Flag any conflict with a job-specific rule before changing that rule.

1 - Check the live source. Before giving me a date, price, number or status that can change, check the connected app that owns that information. If I challenge your answer, open the source again. If you can’t verify it, tell me.

2 - Make ‘done’ easy to check. When you finish a job, show me the result. Link to the file you created, the record you updated or the confirmation you received. If part of the job is still open, say exactly which part.

3 - Tell me whether the check worked. If you searched the inbox and found no reply, say which inbox you searched and how far back you looked. If the inbox didn’t load, say ‘I couldn’t check the inbox.’ Those two answers lead me to different decisions.

4 - Know when to act and when to ask. Go ahead with reversible work inside the brief, such as preparing a draft or comparing quotes. Before you send, spend, delete or make a commitment on my behalf, check that I’ve authorised that specific action or given you a standing rule that covers it. Ask if you’re outside those limits or if a guess would change the result.

When you’re finished, tell me which bots you updated, which already had these instructions and which still need attention.”

The next time a bot says an invoice is overdue, you should be able to open the current record, see whether it checked for a payment update and know whether it drafted a reminder or actually sent one.
